arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: NJ Transit's lawyer argued the system's features answer the classification question decisively.
The challenger's lawyer argued a state creating a new public entity has a choice between a traditional government body and a separate corporation.
NJ Transit's lawyer conceded New Jersey courts are open to claims for events occurring outside of states.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: New Jersey created NJ Transit decades ago to provide what it saw as an essential public good: a statewide public transportation system. The case asks which legal category the system belongs in. The Court heard the dispute together with a consolidated case.

sections.heading: How the case got here
paragraphs: The case reached the Supreme Court after lower-court proceedings. NJ Transit conceded in a footnote to a reply brief that New Jersey courts are open to claims for events occurring outside of states.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: NJ Transit argues its features answer the classification question decisively: it is most like a state agency, not a private business or locality. New Jersey exercised its own autonomy when it created the system.

The challenger argues the state had a choice when it created a new public entity. It could have made a traditional department or agency using state employees, state property, and public money. The challenger says NJ Transit does not fit that mold and relies on a Rule 19 necessary-party analysis.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: NJ Transit disclaims liability for the debts and other exposure of the Transit Authority, a point the Chief Justice raised during questioning.
The challenger's lawyer described the dispute as a Rule 19 necessary party sort of analysis.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor questioned the reliance on control alone, saying the Court has called control a perilous inquiry and that funding percentages matter too.

Justice Thomas asked what the best case is for treating the corporation as having the benefit of sovereignty, and whether anything more recent exists. He noted states historically create corporations to do things they cannot or will not do themselves, like borrow money, run banks, and run businesses.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The ruling will shape how states structure public entities. States can choose between traditional government bodies and separately created corporations, and the classification controls legal exposure.

sections.heading: What the Court decided
paragraphs: NJ Transit is a legally separate corporation responsible for its own debts and judgments, so it is not an arm of New Jersey. Therefore it does not share New Jersey's sovereign immunity from out-of-state lawsuits.
The Pennsylvania Supreme Court's judgment was reversed, the New York Court of Appeals' judgment was affirmed, and both cases were sent back for further proceedings.
